{{Short description|Equation relating to oscillating systems}}
The '''Stuart–Landau equation''' describes the behavior of a nonlinear oscillating system near the [[Hopf bifurcation]], named after [[John Trevor Stuart]] and [[Lev Landau]]. In 1944, [[Lev Landau|Landau]] proposed an equation for the evolution of the magnitude of the disturbance, which is now called as the '''Landau equation''', to explain the transition to [[turbulence]] based on a phenomenological argument<ref>Landau, L. D. (1944). On the problem of turbulence. In Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR (Vol. 44, No. 8, pp. 339-349).</ref> and an attempt to derive this equation from hydrodynamic equations was done by Stuart for [[Hagen–Poiseuille equation#Plane Poiseuille flow|plane Poiseuille flow]] in 1958.<ref>Stuart, J. T. (1958). On the non-linear mechanics of hydrodynamic stability. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 4(1), 1-21.</ref> The formal derivation to derive the ''Landau equation'' was given by Stuart, Watson and Palm in 1960.<ref>Stuart, J. T. (1960). On the non-linear mechanics of wave disturbances in stable and unstable parallel flows Part 1. The basic behaviour in plane Poiseuille flow. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 9(3), 353-370.</ref><ref>Watson, J. (1960). On the non-linear mechanics of wave disturbances in stable and unstable parallel flows Part 2. The development of a solution for plane Poiseuille flow and for plane Couette flow. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 9(3), 371-389.</ref><ref>Palm, E. (1960). On the tendency towards hexagonal cells in steady convection. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 8(2), 183-192.</ref> The perturbation in the vicinity of bifurcation is governed by the following equation

:<math>\frac{dA}{dt} = \sigma A - \frac{l}{2} A |A|^2.</math>

where 
*<math>A = |A| e^{i\phi}</math> is a complex quantity describing the disturbance,
*<math>\sigma = \sigma_r + i\sigma_i</math> is the complex growth rate,
*<math>l = l_r + i l_i</math> is a complex number and <math>l_r</math> is the ''Landau constant''.

The evolution of the actual disturbance is given by the real part of <math>A(t)</math> i.e.,  by <math>|A|\cos\phi</math>. Here the real part of the growth rate is taken to be positive, i.e., <math>\sigma_r>0</math> because otherwise the system is stable in the linear sense, that is to say, for [[infinitesimal]] disturbances (<math>|A|</math> is a small number), the nonlinear term in the above equation is negligible in comparison to the other two terms in which case the amplitude grows in time only if <math>\sigma_r>0</math>. The ''Landau constant'' is also taken to be positive, <math>l_r>0</math> because otherwise the amplitude will grow indefinitely (see below equations and the general solution in the next section). The ''Landau equation'' is the equation for the magnitude of the disturbance,

:<math>\frac{d|A|^2}{dt} = 2\sigma_r |A|^2 - l_r |A|^4,</math>

which can also be re-written as<ref>Provansal, M., Mathis, C., & Boyer, L. (1987). Bénard-von Kármán instability: transient and forced regimes. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 182, 1-22.</ref>

:<math>\frac{d|A|}{dt} = \sigma_r |A| -\frac{l_r}{2} |A|^3.</math>

Similarly, the equation for the phase is given by

:<math>\frac{d\phi}{dt}= \sigma_i-\frac{l_i}{2} |A|^2.</math>

For non-homogeneous systems, i.e., when <math>A</math> depends on spatial coordinates, see [[Ginzburg–Landau equation]]. Due to the universality of the equation, the equation finds its application in many fields such as [[hydrodynamic stability]],<ref>Drazin, P. G., & Reid, W. H. (2004). Hydrodynamic stability. Cambridge university press.</ref> [[Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction]],<ref>Kuramoto, Y. (2012). Chemical oscillations, waves, and turbulence (Vol. 19). Springer Science & Business Media.</ref> etc. 

==General solution==

The ''Landau equation'' is linear when it is written for the dependent variable <math>|A|^{-2}</math>,

:<math>\frac{d|A|^{-2}}{dt} + 2\sigma_r |A|^{-2} = l_r.</math>

The general solution for <math>\sigma_r\neq 0</math> of the above equation is

:<math>|A(t)|^{-2} = \frac{l_r}{2\sigma_r} + \left(|A(0)|^{-2} - \frac{l_r}{2\sigma_r}\right)e^{-2\sigma_r t}.</math>

As <math>t\rightarrow\infty</math>, the magnitude of the disturbance <math>|A|</math> approaches a constant value that is independent of its initial value, i.e., <math>|A|_{\mathrm{max}}\rightarrow(2\sigma_r/l_r)^{1/2}</math> when <math>t\gg 1/\sigma_r</math>. The above solution implies that <math>|A|</math> does not have a real solution if <math>l_r<0</math> and <math>\sigma_r>0</math>. The associated solution for the phase function <math>\phi(t)</math> is given by

:<math>\phi(t)-\phi(0) = \sigma_i t - \frac{l_i}{2l_r} \ln \left[1+ \frac{|A(0)|^2l_r}{2\sigma_r}(e^{2\sigma_r t}-1)\right].</math>

As <math>t\gg 1/\sigma_r</math>, the phase varies linearly with time, <math>\phi \sim (\sigma_i/\sigma_r-l_i/l_r)\sigma_rt.</math>

It is instructive to consider a hydrodynamic stability case where it is found that, according to the [[linear stability]] analysis, the flow is stable when <math>Re\leq Re_{\mathrm{cr}}</math> and unstable otherwise, where <math>Re</math> is the [[Reynolds number]] and the <math>Re_{\mathrm{cr}}</math> is the critical Reynolds number; a familiar example that is applicable here is the critical Reynolds number, <math>Re_{\mathrm{cr}}\approx 50</math>, corresponding to the transition to [[Kármán vortex street]] in the problem of flow past a cylinder.<ref>Schumm, M., Berger, E., & Monkewitz, P. A. (1994). Self-excited oscillations in the wake of two-dimensional bluff bodies and their control. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 271, 17-53.</ref><ref>Dušek, J., Le Gal, P., & Fraunié, P. (1994). A numerical and theoretical study of the first Hopf bifurcation in a cylinder wake. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 264, 59-80.</ref> The growth rate <math>\sigma_r</math> is negative when <math>Re<Re_{\mathrm{cr}}</math> and is positive when <math>Re>Re_{\mathrm{cr}}</math> and therefore in the neighbourhood <math>Re\rightarrow Re_{\mathrm{cr}}</math>, it may written as <math>\sigma_r=\text{const}.\times (Re-Re_{\mathrm{cr}})</math> wherein the constant is positive. Thus, the limiting amplitude is given by

:<math>|A|_{\mathrm{max}} \propto \sqrt{Re-Re_{\mathrm{cr}}}.</math>

==Negative Landau constant==
When the Landau constant is negative, <math>l_r<0</math>, we must include a negative term of higher order to arrest the unbounded increase of the perturbation. In this case, the Landau equation becomes<ref>Landau, L. D. (1959). EM Lifshitz, Fluid Mechanics. Course of Theoretical Physics, 6.</ref>

:<math>\frac{d|A|^2}{dt} = 2\sigma_r |A|^2 - l_r |A|^4 - \beta_r|A|^6, \quad \beta_r>0.</math>

The limiting amplitude then becomes

:<math>|A|_{\mathrm{max}}\rightarrow   \frac{|l_r|}{2\beta_r} \pm \sqrt{\frac{l_r^2}{4\beta_r^2}+\frac{2|l_r|\sigma_r}{\beta_r}}, \quad \text{as} \quad t\gg 1/\sigma_r</math>

where the plus sign corresponds to the stable branch and the minus sign to the unstable branch. There exists a value of a critical value <math>Re_{\mathrm{cr}}'</math> where the above two roots are equal (<math>\sigma_r = -|l_r|/8\beta_r</math>) such that <math>Re_{\mathrm{cr}}'<Re_{\mathrm{cr}}</math>, indicating that the flow in the region <math>Re_{\mathrm{cr}}'<Re<Re_{\mathrm{cr}}</math> is ''metastable'', that is to say, in the metastable region, the flow is stable to infinitesimal perturbations, but not to finite amplitude perturbations.
